description_full: Public Storage is a REIT that primarily acquires, develops, owns, and operates self-storage facilities. At September 30, 2026, the firm: (i) owned and/or operated 4,764 self-storage facilities with approximately 339 million net rentable square feet located in 42 states, Puerto Rico and Canada and (ii) owned a 35% common equity interest in Shurgard Self Storage Limited, which owned 338 self-storage facilities located in seven Western European countries with approximately 19 million net rentable square feet operated under the Shurgard brand. Public Storage headquarters are in Frisco, Texas. Public Storage was incorporated in 1972 in Maryland.
ceo_bio: Mr. H. Thomas Boyle III | CEO & Trustee | Age 41 | Compensation: $2.0M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 5K people. Revenue per employee of $836K ranks in the below the sector median among Real Estate peers, with revenue growing 7%/yr across its filed history. Stock-based compensation of $7K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Public Storage is a large-cap real estate business with a $62.1B market cap on $4.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 14% against a 8% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 73% confirm genuine pricing power.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.9×.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 9.6% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 104% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Payout ratio looks stretched — the dividend’s own margin of safety is thin
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Interest-rate sensitivity and tenant-credit risk — cap rates and refinancing costs move faster than the 10-year leases can absorb.
Remote work structural vacancy — the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work has permanently impaired demand for urban office space across most markets.
Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 21% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
38 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Real Estate peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 43% operating margin runs 21pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.19x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 1.3% of sector revenue and 2.9% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 23% and a beta of 0.77, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $242.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 30% in the 2020 crash, 31% in the 2022 bear market and 52% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $163 (margin of safety -104%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 37%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Real Estate peers: P/E 35.0 vs 23.9 and EV/EBITDA 22.5 vs 16.2 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 45% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an EBIT/EV of 2.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 18 covering analysts target $341 on average, 3% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 8.1%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.24).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.79x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 66%.
ROE of 19% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.8% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.1x net debt to EBITDA ($318.1M of cash against $10.3B of debt), with interest covered 6.9x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.9% over 3 years, 10.6% over 5 years and 7.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Free cash flow has compounded 4.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 9.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (6.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 9.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 84%.
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (3.6% in dividends).
It pays out 126% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 5,770 employees, each generates about $836K of revenue, 0.4x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 7.0% a year across its filed history.
CEO pay is $2.0M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
